query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Synchronous thermal decomposition of a chemically homogeneous single-source precursor drives the formation of HEA nanoparticles by ensuring all noble metal species are released and reduced simultaneously.
generation.material_initial_state: A crystalline single-source precursor in which multiple noble metal coordination complexes are uniformly integrated at the atomic level.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled thermal treatment on the single-source precursor under a reductive gas flow versus using a physical mixture of separate metal salts.
generation.conditions: Moderate heating under reductive atmosphere (e.g., at around 500°C) where synchronized decomposition is enabled by the design of the precursor and enforced by a rapidly reducing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The inherent atomic-level uniformity within the single-source precursor, which ensures the simultaneous liberation of all metal species upon reduction.
generation.mechanism: Coupled liberation and reduction of all metal constituents in a single-step decomposition process prevents sequential nucleation; the reductive atmosphere further supports immediate alloying, yielding a uniform, single-phase nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles derived from the single-source precursor will contain a homogeneous distribution of noble metals in a single-phase alloy, whereas those obtained from individual metal salt mixtures will likely show phase segregation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized from conventional mixtures of metal salts that typically exhibit sequential reduction and phase heterogeneity.
generation.boundary: Effective when the precursor chemistry is precisely tuned for synchronized decomposition; not applicable if even the homogeneous precursor exhibits staggered decomposition kinetics due to ligand or valence state discrepancies.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how robust the method is against slight variations in precursor synthesis and whether minor differences in decomposition kinetics could still induce inhomogeneity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two samples: one from a well-characterized single-source precursor (validated via TGA/DSC for synchronous decomposition) and another from an equivalent physical mixture of individual metal salts. Decompose both under identical thermal profiles in a reductive atmosphere.
measurements: STEM-EDX mapping to assess elemental homogeneity
Thermogravimetric analysis to compare decomposition profiles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-source precursor does not produce significantly more homogeneous and single-phase nanoparticles compared to the mixed-salt sample, the hypothesis of synchronous decomposition is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy oxide nanoparticles (HEO NPs) with multiple component elements possess improved stability and multiple uses for functional applications, including catalysis, data memory, and energy storage. However, the synthesis of homogenous HEO NPs containing five or more immiscible elements with a single-phase structure is still a great challenge due to the strict synthetic conditions. In particular, several synthesis methods of HEO NPs require extremely high temperatures. In this study, we demonstrate a low cost, facile, and effective method to synthesize three- to eight-element HEO nanoparticles by a combination of electrospinning and low-temperature ambient annealing. HEO NPs were generated by annealing nanofibers at 330 °C for 30 minutes under air conditions. The average size of the HEO nanoparticles was ∼30 nm and homogenous element distribution was obtained from post-electrospinning thermal decomposition. The synthesized HEO NPs exhibited magnetic properties with the highest saturation magnetization at 9.588 emu g−1 and the highest coercivity at 147.175 Oe for HEO NPs with four magnetic elements while integrating more nonmagnetic elements will suppress the magnetic response.

As discussed in the introduction, the present study aims to investigate the drivers that favor the formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles at low temperatures. The employed synthesis was first described by Yusenko et al., where a crystalline, single-source precursor is precipitated from metal salt solutions and thermally decomposed in a reductive gas flow while heating to 500 °C. The single-source precursor is a complex salt comprised of coordination compounds of anionic and cationic complexes ([M3+(NH3)5Cl][M4+Cl6]), see also Fig. S2 (ESI†). By introducing variations of M4+ = Os, Ir, Pt, and M3+ = Ir, Rh, Ru, respectively, the mixing of metals occurs on the local level of the crystalline precursor. Thermolysis in an H2-containing gas stream leads to metal reduction, and NH4Cl evaporates. Further details on the synthesis and precursor are given in the ESI.† The synthesis approach can yield single-phase HEA nanoparticles and is thus ideally suited as a model system to study the decisive factors for single-phase formation. As shown in Table S2, the thermal decomposition of the five metal salts occurs at different temperatures. Figure 3a shows the temperature profile along the depth. Once the thermal decomposition temperature (TD) of the metal precursor is reached but below the melting temperature (TM) of the corresponding metals, the thermal decomposition of the mixed metal salt particles adsorbed on the LIG occurs accompanied by gas release, and then each CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticle with homogeneous composition is generated by nucleation and growth of the species from the decomposition of each mixed metal salt particle. This particle is likely to be at the site of the original metal salt particle (the light green zone in Fig. 3a). When the temperature is above TM while below the boiling temperature (TB) of metals, the metallic elements are in the liquid phase to form molten beads. Since metals are nonwetting with carbon, these liquid metal beads tend to aggregate and grow bigger to minimize their surface energy at high temperatures.
